## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Human genome project — objectives and significance

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

The **Human Genome Project (HGP)** was the biggest single project in biology: an international, publicly funded effort (launched 1990, DOE + NIH, James Watson first head) to read the complete sequence of the human genome — all ~3.1 billion base pairs — plus the genomes of model organisms. A private competitor (Celera, Craig Venter, 1998) raced it using shotgun sequencing; both published a draft together in **February 2001**, and the 'complete' reference sequence was declared in **April 2003**.

**Concept flow — the HGP from idea to finished genome (study in this order)**

| Step | Milestone | Year | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Idea proposed at DOE meetings | 1985–86 | Detecting radiation-induced mutations motivated sequencing |
| 2 | HGP officially launched | 1990 | DOE + NIH; 15-year, $3-billion plan; Watson first director |
| 3 | Model organisms sequenced in parallel | 1996–2000 | Yeast (1996), C. elegans (1998), Drosophila (2000) |
| 4 | Celera Genomics enters the race | 1998 | Whole-genome shotgun sequencing vs the clone-by-clone map |
| 5 | Working draft announced jointly | June 2000 / Feb 2001 | Clinton + Blair announcement; papers in Nature (public) and Science (Celera) |
| 6 | 'Complete' reference sequence | April 2003 | 99.99% accurate, essentially all euchromatic DNA |
| 7 | Truly telomere-to-telomere genome | 2022 | T2T consortium closed the last gaps with long-read sequencing |

**HGP goals vs the methods that met them**

| Goal | Method used |
|---|---|
| Identify all ~20,000–25,000 human genes | cDNA/EST mapping + gene prediction |
| Determine the sequence of all 3.1 billion base pairs | Clone-by-clone (BAC contigs) + Sanger sequencing; Celera used shotgun |
| Improve sequencing tools and cost | Automated capillary sequencers, bioinformatics (BLAST era) |
| Sequence model organisms (E. coli, yeast, worm, fly, mouse) | Parallel comparative-genomics tracks |
| Address ethics, legal and social issues (ELSI) | 5% of budget reserved — the first project with a built-in ethics arm |
| Store everything in free public databases | GenBank / EMBL / DDBJ — data released within 24 h (Bermuda Principles) |

**Significance of the HGP — classified by field**

| Field | Impact |
|---|---|
| Medicine | Genetic testing, carrier screening, pharmacogenomics (drug response by genotype), cancer genomics |
| Basic biology | Gene number (~20k, fewer than rice), gene families, non-coding RNA, regulatory elements mapped |
| Evolution | Human–chimp–mouse comparisons; conserved vs diverged regions; 'Out of Africa' genomic evidence |
| Technology | Sequencing cost fell from ~$3 billion to under $1,000 — the basis of today's genomic medicine |
| Forensics and identity | STR profiling standards, mitochondrial DNA databases |
| Ethics (ELSI) | GINA-type genetic-discrimination law, privacy of genetic data, informed consent standards |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — what the numbers taught us.** Before the HGP, estimates of human gene count ran to 100,000. The finished sequence revealed roughly **20,000–25,000** protein-coding genes — fewer than rice — while ~98% of the genome does NOT code for protein. The lesson: complexity comes less from gene count and more from regulation, alternative splicing and non-coding RNA. This single surprise redirected a decade of biology.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: HGP facts: 1990–2003, 3.2 billion base pairs, ~20,000–25,000 genes, international consortium (US, UK, Japan, France, Germany, China) — the numbers are the marks.
Trick 2: Two approaches: expressed sequence tags (EST) and sequence annotation; methods: Sanger sequencing + BAC/YAC clones + overlaps.
Trick 3: Findings to quote: only ~2% codes for proteins; genes are unevenly distributed; SNP mapping; ~1.4 million SNPs identified.
Trick 4: Significance: medicine (gene therapy, pharmacogenomics), forensics, evolutionary comparison — three applications.
